source.title: How do Funeral Practices Impact Bereaved Relatives' Mental Health, Grief and Bereavement? A Mixed Methods Review with Implications for COVID-19

A rapid review of 17 studies of variable quality; cards say where evidence is mixed. Cards are our own summaries; no quotes.

cards.title: Missing a funeral does not decide how your grief will go
cards.body:
If you could not attend a funeral, or it was not the farewell you wanted, it is natural to worry about what that means for your grief. This review gathered 17 studies on funeral practices and the wellbeing of bereaved people.

The research was mixed. Five observational studies found benefits from taking part in funerals, and six found no measurable link. Taken together, there is no clear evidence that how a funeral goes, or whether you were there, determines how you will grieve over time. Many other things shape that journey, including the support around you.
cards.apply_it: If you could not be at a funeral, consider writing a short letter to the person who died, saying what you would have said there.

quiz.question: What did the review find about funeral participation and later grief?
options: The evidence was mixed and inconclusive
Missing a funeral always leads to worse grief
No studies had looked at it
quiz.explanation: Five observational studies found benefits and six did not, so the evidence was inconclusive.

cards.title: What seems to help is a goodbye that feels meaningful to you
cards.body:
Interviews and personal accounts in the review added something the numbers could not. For both adults and children, rituals after a death helped most when the bereaved could shape them and say goodbye in a way that felt meaningful to them.

So there is no single right way to mourn. A large formal service, a quiet gathering at home, a walk to a favourite place or a shared meal can all be meaningful. What matters is that it feels true to you and to the person you have lost.
cards.apply_it: Think about one small thing that would feel like a fitting goodbye for you, such as a place, a song or a meal, and plan it.

quiz.question: According to the qualitative research, what makes after-death rituals helpful?
options: Having as many guests as possible
Keeping them as short as possible
Being able to shape them and say goodbye in a meaningful way
quiz.explanation: The benefit depends on the ability of the bereaved to shape rituals and say goodbye in a way that is meaningful to them.

cards.title: The same ritual can comfort one person and overwhelm another
cards.body:
In a study of mourners in Turkey, a tradition of never leaving the bereaved alone was felt as supportive by some and as difficult, even disturbing, by others. The difference was a sense of control. People who kept some personal space and a say in what happened found it comforting. Those who felt they had no control, often older people who depended on others, found it harder.

If you are supporting someone who is grieving, offer company rather than insisting on it, and let them shape what happens.
cards.apply_it: If you are supporting someone grieving, ask them what would help today rather than assuming, and respect the answer.

quiz.question: What determined whether the 'never leave them alone' ritual felt helpful?
options: The mourner's sense of control and personal space
quiz.explanation: Participants who kept a sense of personal space and control found it supportive; others found it difficult.

cards.title: Being involved in planning helped some people, but not everyone
cards.body:
In one study, more than half of bereaved people felt that planning the funeral helped their grief, while others were unsure, and some saw it as a routine duty. Another study found that people who took part in planning reported less social isolation and less of a sense of unreality afterwards.

So involvement can help, but it should be an offer, not a burden. If you want to take part, choosing a reading, a song or a photo can be a way to put love into the goodbye. If it feels too much, it is fine to let others carry it.
cards.apply_it: If a funeral is being planned, choose one small part you would like to contribute, or tell someone you would rather not be involved.

quiz.question: In one study, how did people feel about planning the funeral?
options: Over half felt it helped, while others were unsure or found it unhelpful
quiz.explanation: 57% felt planning helped, 28% were unsure, and 15% found it unhelpful.

cards.title: Showing up for someone's funeral is support they may remember for years
cards.body:
In interviews, bereaved relatives saw a large turnout as a sign of support that stayed helpful for years afterwards, while a small turnout could feel like a lack of support. The authors conclude that funerals help partly by showing the bereaved that people care.

If you have been unsure whether to go to a funeral because you did not know the person well, or fear intruding, this suggests your presence can matter. A card, a message or a visit later can carry the same message if you cannot be there.
cards.apply_it: Think of someone who has been bereaved recently. Send them a short message or note today letting them know you are thinking of them.

quiz.question: How did bereaved relatives view high funeral attendance?
options: As supportive, and helpful for years afterwards
quiz.explanation: High funeral attendance was felt as supportive and remained helpful for years afterwards.

cards.title: Conflict around a funeral can weigh on grief, so protect the peace
cards.body:
In one US study, mourners who described the funeral as comforting reported less grief, isolation, despair, anger and guilt. Problems during the service, such as conflict between relatives or clashes between the wishes of the person who died and those of the family, were linked to heavier grief.

These are associations, so the cause is not clear. Still, grief is hard enough without added conflict. Where you can, it may help to talk openly about wishes, let some disagreements go for now, and keep the focus on remembering together.
cards.apply_it: If tensions are rising around arrangements, suggest one shared priority everyone agrees on, such as honouring a particular wish.

quiz.question: What was linked to heavier grief in one US study?
options: Conflict and adverse events during the funeral
quiz.explanation: Adverse events such as conflicts among survivors were associated with higher overall grief.

cards.title: A small, simple funeral can be just as meaningful
cards.body:
During the pandemic many funerals had to be small. The authors concluded that what makes a funeral supportive is not the number of people or the type of service, but how meaningful it feels and how connected it helps mourners feel. Another study they mention found no link between how elaborate a cremation service was and levels of grief.

A report from the pandemic period described people who attended smaller funerals appreciating how intimate and personal they were. If a farewell was smaller than you hoped, its value lies in the love in it, not its size.
cards.apply_it: If a farewell was smaller than you wanted, plan a later gathering or memorial where more people can share memories.

quiz.question: According to the authors, what matters more than the size of a funeral?
options: How meaningful it is and how connected mourners feel
quiz.explanation: It is not the number of attendees or type of funeral, but how meaningful it is and how connected people feel.

cards.title: The funeral is one moment in a much longer grief
cards.body:
An Australian study found that six weeks after a death, people who had viewed the body or said goodbye as they wished had fewer depressive symptoms and less intense grief. By six months and thirteen months, these differences were no longer visible. In a Dutch study, how grief felt at six months mattered more for grief three years later than how the funeral was rated.

Funerals can bring comfort in the early weeks, but they are not the whole story. Grief unfolds over a long time, and the support you receive along the way matters too.
cards.apply_it: Mark a date a few months from now to check in on someone who is grieving, when the early support has often faded.

quiz.question: What happened to the early benefits of viewing the body or saying goodbye as wished?
options: They were no longer evident at 6 and 13 months
quiz.explanation: The associations seen at 6 weeks were not evident at 6 months or 13 months.

cards.title: Children may benefit from being included in mourning, with choice
cards.body:
Two studies found that children and adults bereaved as children who had less chance to take part in mourning activities had more depressive symptoms later. These findings come with caveats about how the studies were analysed, and another small study found no link.

Accounts from teenagers were mixed too. Some resented being involved and found it harder to cope, while others felt it brought the family closer. A gentle approach is to explain what will happen, invite children to take part, and let them choose how much.
cards.apply_it: If a child is affected by a death, explain simply what will happen at the funeral and ask whether, and how, they would like to take part.
cards.locator: Results: Children's bereavement outcomes and experiences

quiz.question: What do the studies suggest about children and mourning activities?
options: Less opportunity to take part was linked with more depressive symptoms, though views varied
Children should always be kept away
Children are never affected by funerals
quiz.explanation: Less opportunity to participate was associated with more depressive symptoms, but teenagers' views were mixed.

cards.title: Children valued personal touches and the support of others
cards.body:
When children were asked what they liked about a parent's funeral, common answers were the music, especially the person's favourite song, flowers, prayers and poems, putting something into the casket, the eulogy and the support of others. Some also valued the sense of finality.

What they disliked included how some adults behaved, seeing the body, and a minister who did not know their parent. These answers offer gentle guidance: give children small, personal ways to take part, and prepare them for anything that might be hard to see.
cards.apply_it: Invite a grieving child to choose something personal, such as a drawing, a letter or a song, to be part of the farewell.
cards.locator: Results: Children's bereavement outcomes and experiences

quiz.question: Which of these did children commonly say they liked about the funeral?
options: A leader who did not know their parent
The person's favourite song and putting something in the casket
quiz.explanation: Children liked aspects such as the person's favourite song, flowers, poems, putting something in the casket and the support of others.

cards.title: If you cannot be there, there are other ways to take part
cards.body:
People who could not attend a funeral because of distance described distress about it. During the pandemic, live-streaming and other ways of including absent mourners became common, and one participant described joining a parent's funeral from abroad as a positive experience. Some religious leaders noted that streaming widened access for people who could not usually attend.

The review found no studies yet on how virtual attendance affects grief, so this is still an open question. But joining remotely, or holding your own small ritual at the same time, can help you feel part of the goodbye.
cards.apply_it: If you cannot travel to a funeral, ask whether it can be streamed, or light a candle and share memories with someone at the same time.

quiz.question: What does the review say about virtual funeral attendance?
options: It is proven to harm grief
It is proven to be as good as attending
No studies yet measured its effect on grief, though some accounts were positive
quiz.explanation: The review found no literature on how virtual attendance affects outcomes, though one account was positive.

cards.title: Personal, family-led services may serve grief better than templates
cards.body:
The authors suggest that template services, where the officiant leads everything, may be less fitting than personalised services where the family takes the lead and the officiant helps them create their own rituals.

They also note that funeral providers can be an important source of support. In one Australian survey, bereaved people rated their support as helpful, second only to support from family. If you are arranging a funeral, it is reasonable to ask for something that reflects the person, and to lean on the professionals helping you.
cards.apply_it: If you are arranging a farewell, tell the funeral provider or celebrant three things that made the person who they were.

quiz.question: Which approach do the authors suggest may be more appropriate?
options: Strict template services led by the officiant
Personalised services where families lead and the officiant facilitates
Services with no officiant at all
quiz.explanation: Personalised, family-led services with the officiant facilitating may be more appropriate than template services.
